title: Hackers Abuse Sliver, Mimikatz and Ethereum C2 in Windows Post-Exploitation Attack
content_md: A Windows post-exploitation toolkit linked to a ransomware investigation used reverse shells, credential theft utilities , service masquerading and Ethereum-based command-and-control infrastructure to maintain access inside a targeted network. The investigation initially classified two dozen numbered binaries as probable Sliver implants. However, later analysis found that the files were not Sliver payloads. They were plain reverse shells designed to provide attackers with remote command execution on compromised Windows systems. This correction is important because the first analysis relied on a limited review method. Analysts used a string-tokenisation approach that failed to identify addresses stored inside Go language pooled string blobs. As a result, the binaries were incorrectly reported as containing no command-and-control addresses. Further inspection showed that every analysed reverse shell contained its own C2 address in clear text. The addresses were not hidden through encryption or complex obfuscation. Instead, they were missed because the extraction method could not view the relevant substring within the compiled Go binary data. The case highlights a common incident-response issue, an empty result does not always confirm the absence of malicious content. Detection and forensic tools must clearly state what data they inspected, what formats they support and where their visibility ends.
